title: Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice
summary: Listen at your own pace, with the guidance available alongside.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.chapter: Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice
turns.text: An equity goal describes a change worth working toward. The practical question is how the work in front of us could contribute to that change. A course, a tool, or a team conversation can help, but its value depends on what people are able to do with it afterward. Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice introduces a simple way to explain that relationship.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.chapter: Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice
turns.text: You will use a logic model: a description of the knowledge and resources available, the work people do, what that work produces, and the change it is intended to support. The model is useful because it makes the connection open to discussion. It does not make the intended result happen automatically. In the service example, staff knowledge and community accounts inform a review of a service-change notice. The review produces a clearer draft.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.chapter: Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice
turns.text: The intended result is that readers can understand and use the next step. Those are connected, but they are different. A clear draft may still need review, release, a usable way to reach people, and a working response route. If any of those conditions fails, the intended benefit may not reach the reader. The course connects this reasoning with the Aging and Disability Services Administration's six equity goal areas.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.chapter: Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice
turns.text: They concern eliminating disparities, community engagement, hiring and retention, learning and development, contracts and procurement, and communication and accessibility. The goals relate to one another. A service communication may benefit from staff learning and community participation as well as clearer wording. A workforce opportunity may involve recruitment, development, and attention to disparities at the same time. DSD can choose approaches that fit its work while remaining aligned with the plan and relevant requirements.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.chapter: Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice
turns.text: You do not need to force every activity under every goal. Nor should a useful equity question disappear because it does not fit neatly beneath one heading. The starting point is the actual concern and the change the team can help bring about. The workplace example considers a clearer development invitation. Learning and employee perspectives inform a review, and the team produces a better invitation. That does not guarantee that people can take part.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.chapter: Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice
turns.text: Scheduling, preparation, workload, and the learning arrangement may still matter. A logic model helps a supervisor see those conditions instead of treating the completed communication as the entire result. Community knowledge also helps define what a useful result means. In the course, a participant says the service notice still leaves the response route unclear. If staff have defined success only as fewer questions, they may miss the concern.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.chapter: Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice
turns.text: The more useful inquiry is whether people understand the next step and can use it. Their experience may change the outcome the team should pay attention to. By the end, you will write one clear connection between a goal, a relevant learning or work activity, and a change you hope to support. You will identify the assumptions that need checking and the responsibilities involved.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.chapter: Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice
turns.text: The purpose is a practical explanation colleagues can use together: why this work matters, what it contributes, and what would help you understand whether that contribution is making a difference. Consider a reader who receives the revised notice but still cannot find the next step. The notice exists; the intended benefit is uncertain. In your model, connect staff learning with the wording change, then ask what the reader can understand and do.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.chapter: Connecting Equity Goals, Learning, and Everyday Practice
turns.text: If the contact route is unusable, another wording edit may not solve the problem. This is how the model helps you choose where attention belongs, while keeping the reader’s experience central.
